area.Bigger: The answer was bigger than your guess, comparing both at their peak.
area.Smaller: The answer was smaller than your guess, comparing both at their peak.
area.Approximate: The answer and your guess were about the same size at their peak, within 10%.

era.Bigger: The answer is more recent: its peak came after your guess's peak.
era.Smaller: The answer is older: its peak came before your guess's peak.
era.Approximate: The answer and your guess are from the same era: each still existed at the other's peak, or their peaks were 25 years apart or less.

distance.info: Where the answer lies from your guess. When the two are apart, you get the direction and the distance between their borders. When the territories overlap, you get how much they share, and the direction goes away once they mostly overlap. When one lies almost entirely inside the other, you get Inside your guess or Contains your guess.
distance.here: Here: the answer lies {direction} of your guess.
distance.noMap: No map to compare where these two are.
distance.spreadAnswer: The answer's territory is spread over far-apart places, so no arrow would really point to it.
distance.spreadGuess: Your guess's territory is spread over far-apart places, so no arrow would really start from it.
distance.spreadBoth: Both are spread over far-apart places, so no arrow would make sense.
distance.arrowFlat: The arrow follows the flat map.
distance.arrowGlobe: The arrow follows the globe: it's the shortest route, which on the flat map may look like another direction.

fieldInfo.era: The broad period of history in which the peak took place. It's a rough division, built around European history, and doesn't always fit other parts of the world well.
fieldInfo.mapConfidence: For most of history, the borders of kingdoms and empires weren't exact lines. Many maps are just approximations of the area under control, and some are reconstructions based on little evidence.
fieldInfo.continents: Continents where it held territory at its peak.
fieldInfo.capital: Some empires changed capitals over time, had more than one at once, or had no fixed capital at all. This is the best-known capital or main city.
fieldInfo.language: The main language of the government and the elite. Many empires brought together dozens of peoples and languages.
fieldInfo.referenceYear: The year of the greatest territorial extent, which is what the map shows. Other factors, like stability or prosperity, aren't taken into account.
fieldInfo.period: From its rise to its end. Start and end dates are often debated by historians, so the most widely accepted ones are used.
fieldInfo.area: The largest area ever controlled. Estimates of historical area vary a lot between sources, so treat it as an order of magnitude.
fieldInfo.religion: The official religion, or that of the ruling elite, not necessarily that of most of the population.
fieldInfo.curiosity: A striking fact about the answer. Usually the most revealing clue.

clueValues.mapContinents: The map now shows the continents
clueValues.mapCountries: The map now shows the countries

clueInfo.mapContinents: The map now shows the continents under the answer. You can go back to the outline with the picker right under the map.
clueInfo.mapCountries: The map now shows today's countries under the answer. Tap a country to see its name.
clueInfo.curiosity: A curiosity about the answer. The three go from the least to the most obvious.

About.title: About
About.what: Imperatle is a daily guessing game. Every day, an empire or other historical power appears on the map, at the height of its expansion, and you try to figure out which one it is.
About.editorial: The game is only about territorial extent and facts. Showing how far an empire reached isn't celebrating conquest: many of them grew through war, colonization and the suffering of other peoples.
About.sources: Historical borders are adapted from <clio>Cliopatria</clio> (Bennett et al., Seshat Global History Databank), under <license>CC BY 4.0</license>, simplified and adjusted to today's coastline. The world map comes from <ne>Natural Earth</ne> (public domain). Historical dates, areas and borders are approximations, and sources often disagree.
About.author: Made by <link>Ventura</link>, a developer from Brazil.

AboutPage.title: About Imperatle
AboutPage.description: What Imperatle is, the daily game of guessing empires from their maps: how it works, frequently asked questions, map sources and who made it.
AboutPage.intro1: Imperatle is a daily history and geography game. Every day, an empire or another historical power shows up on the map, drawn at the height of its expansion, and you have 7 attempts to find out which one it is.
AboutPage.intro2: There are {count} empires and powers, from antiquity to the 20th century: from Rome, Persia and Han China to the Mongols, the Inca, the Khmer Empire and the European colonial empires. The game is free, needs no sign-up and is in English, Portuguese and Spanish.
AboutPage.how: Each wrong guess compares your pick with the answer: whether it was bigger or smaller at its peak, older or more recent, and how far away and in which direction it lies. Each miss also unlocks a clue: first the era, then the map with the continents, three curiosities and, last, the map with today's countries. At the end of the round you get the answer's full fact sheet, with capital, language, religion, dates, area and the historical context.

free.a: Yes. The daily challenge is free forever. Anyone who wants to support the project makes a one-time payment and gets practice mode and past games.

account.a: No. Without one, your progress and stats stay in your browser. Signing in with Google keeps your stats and shows the same ones on your phone and your computer.

when.q: When is there a new challenge?
when.a: Every day, at midnight Brasília time (3 a.m. UTC).

powers.a: Because not every great power in history was called an empire: there are caliphates, dynasties, kingdoms and republics, such as the Abbasid Caliphate, the Song Dynasty and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth.

maps.q: Where do the maps come from?
maps.a: The historical borders are adapted from Cliopatria (Seshat Global History Databank), and the world map comes from Natural Earth. Old borders are always approximate, and each map states its own precision.

more.q: Can I play past days or practise?
more.a: Yes, as a supporter: past games bring back the challenge of any day gone by, and practice mode draws empires as often as you like, with era, continent and difficulty filters, without touching your stats.

list.q: Is there a list of the empires in the game?
list.a: Yes, on the <link>Empires</link> page, with each one's fact sheet and curiosities.

mistake.q: I found a mistake. How do I report it?
mistake.a: With the feedback button in the menu. Every historical correction is welcome.
